utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis along with Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic and Eugene O'Sullivan, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the witness resumes the stand, there are two matters which the -- I'm sorry, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. My presence was not noted in the transcript. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. There are two matters which the Chamber wishes to raise. I would invite Judge Harhoff to deal with one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 22nd of June, the Chamber directed the Zupljanin Defence to liaise directly with the Prosecution when it is able to confirm whether any of its witnesses are willing to meet with the Prosecution. And we further directed that the Prosecution would do what is necessary to bring it formally before the Chamber, if further intervention were necessary. The Chamber understands that such an update was indeed informally communicated amongst the parties. But we would ask you, Mr. Krgovic, just to state for the record the position of your witnesses on this issue. Are you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is no change in this position, nor our witness is willing to meet with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I inquire because the last message I recall seing about this there was an indication that there were three witnesses, SZ-004, 005 and 001, who had not been contacted. I just wondered if that was still the same, or if they have been contacted and indicated they don't want to talk to us either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My understanding from Mr. Krgovic's answer was that none of the witnesses to be called by Zupljanin are willing -- Is that correct, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You are correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, following from this, the Chamber recalls that, also on the 22nd of June, the Prosecution had made a formal application to have this fact considered a relevant factor when addressing its request for cross-examination under Rule 92 bis (C) on the Zupljanin motion for the admission of the statements of these witnesses. We would like to invite the Prosecution to substantiate its request by putting forth a reasoned argument as to how the unwillingness of the ten character witnesses to speak or to meet with the Prosecutor's office is a relevant fact under 92 bis (C). It should provide the reference to any authority that you have on this subject, if possible. And, Mr. Hannis, do you think you could provide us with a reason during the course this day?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I guess I would request permission to have a day to file something in writing for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You wouldn't have to do it in writing, just orally would be fine. But we need to be sure that we have understood fully the background and the reasons for your request.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And it relates to the 92 bis witnesses who -- to the extent that they are character witnesses, their statements are in the general nature of, I knew Mr. Zupljanin many years and he never said a bad thing about a non-Serb. Well, our position is that goes to the acts and conduct of the accused which is a factor that leans in favour of having that witness appear. Because how else are we going to be able to explore the basis for their opinion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That wasn't the point, Mr. Hannis. If I understood Ms. Korner correctly, she said that the fact that the witnesses had refused to speak to you was, in itself, something that would favour their being called for cross-examination, and it is this argument that we are interested in understanding better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In a way, Your Honour, it's like trying to prove the negative. Without being able to speak to them, we don't know. If we spoke to them, we might be satisfied this is a person who knew him but only knew him in this limited extent, and therefore we don't have a problem with their opinion being expressed because it won't carry much weight. But with not being able to speak to them, we have no idea about that. And neither will the Court, frankly. I think you need that information to weigh their evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, does this exhaust your answer to my question, or would you still need more time to consider it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have more time to consult with Ms. Korner to see if she had some additional input.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: By the end of the day, if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. The second matter is more of a housekeeping nature. When the witness returns to the stand this morning, I intend to inform him that the -- having consulted with VWS through the kind assistance of the Court Officer, we have decided that in order to accommodate his peculiar circumstances, we would vary the sitting times so that we sit in sessions of an hour each with a 15 minute break. So, therefore, we would sit from 9.00 to 10.00, from 10.15 to 11.15, 11.30 to 12.30, and 12.45 to 1.45, which, arithmetically, we trust should still keep us within the four hours permitted each day. And this also means that everyone concerned - and, in that, I include the Judges - would have to impose the discipline on themselves to return at the end of 15 minutes. But before that is communicated to the witness, I just wondered whether counsel had a view on the varied sitting times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no problem with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No problem with that either, Your Honours, and I'm grateful to the Trial Chamber for that. Because I see that the witness is having problems sitting longer than ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And you, likewise, Mr. Krgovic, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we're grateful to counsel for their co-operation in this matter. So if there's nothing else that -- to delay us, could the witness be returned to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, good morning to you, sir. Welcome back. I trust you are recovered from yesterday. Before Mr. Zecevic continues his examination-in-chief, there are two matters. First of all, is what would become the usual reminder that the Chamber would give that you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The second matter is that you would recall that at the beginning of yesterday, I explained to you how the sessions are broken up in the -- how the day's sitting is broken up into sessions. Taking into consideration your peculiar circumstances, it has been decided that we will sit in hourly sessions with a 15 minute break in between. And we have been informed through VWS that that would suffice. So the first break then would be at 10.00 this morning. And we would have a 15-minute break, and then resume for another hour and so on, until we come to the end of the day's sitting at 1.45. I trust that this works out for you and everyone concerned. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Mr. Macar, before we go back to yesterday's topic, we have two corrections for the transcript. Page 22860, yesterday's LiveNote, you were saying that in parallel to the establishment of the administration in the ministry's HQ, it was necessary to get help for the setting up of the centres of the security services that did not exist prior to April 1992. And then you named a total of five, those that didn't exist and those that did in fact exist. But this didn't come across with any clarity at all.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before April 1992, the ones that didn't exist were Sarajevo, that is, the Sarajevo-Birac-Romanija region, Bijeljina, and Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And which were the ones that did exist?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sarajevo public security centre --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Just take it easy, please. When I ask that the ones that did exist, I mean Security Services Centres of the MUP of the RBiH those that did exist before 1992 and that now became part of the MUP of the RBiH.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Banja Luka and Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At page 22867, I asked you about the situation at Pale and at Sokolac at the time. And you said in one word: A disaster. You talked about Sokolac. Can you tell us more about Pale and the situation there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having arrived at Pale in the last quarter of April 1992, the situation was very much alike. There were lots of people coming in as refugees. The local economy was in tatters. There was nothing to buy in shops. It was very chaotic. The municipal authorities had nowhere to put up these people arriving. People would wander around parks looking for a place to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation regarding the electricity and water supplies, as well as the telephone lines?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No electricity in Pale. I know because the building when I arrived, say, on or about the 20th of April, the electricity supply had been cut off. The same thing applied to the water supply, and there was probably a casual link between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 22867, you said: "The Muslim forces left us two or three telephone lines because those lines went through the central post office in Sarajevo. There were those two or three telephone lines that they could eavesdrop on. We used those lines for our communications." As you say, lines went through the central post office in Sarajevo, but were those phone lines cut as well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They weren't. Probably for the reasons that I listed because they were using these lines to eavesdrop on our communications. There were several dozens of telephone lines in the Vrace area that were operating but for no longer than a couple of days. All of them were cut off, save for two or three of them in one building and there was a third telephone line in the building in which I was staying, and two in the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know about the fact that the other side were listening onto your conversations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were ten or 15 phone lines to begin with, and they left only two. So if you add two and two together ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How did you use those phone lines then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The line I was using, in nine out of ten cases, were used by inspectors to get in touch with their families, to check the situation. In emergencies, we used it for professional purposes, for our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I promised that I would try and remember the date when the incident occurred in Milici. You remember me explaining about the courier system that we used and the reason I remember that day. The incident occurred at Milici when those people were ambushed and the boksit company drivers were killed there. I was a part of that column and then I turned off to go and deliver mail to someone, thereby avoiding the incident. That happened on the 27th of May, 1992. The reason I remember is because on 25th of May, I was staying at Vrace and then I was on my way to visit a family in Vojkovici. I wanted to wash there and get some civilian clothes so that I could press on to Belgrade. On that occasion, at one point along the Vrace-Vojkovic road, there was a car that was struck by a bullet which then ricocheted and hit yet another car. There were two of us in the car. The 25th was also the Youth Day in the former Yugoslavia. So the first time the bullet hit that car along that road. Two days later, I was headed for Belgrade on through Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, we talked yesterday about documents that you had a chance to see after your arrival at the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 798D1, which is tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the header reads: "Federal Secretariat of the Interior." You have the number there. The date is the 22nd of April, 1992. Subject: State commission for genocide, responsibilities of the OUP, internal affairs organ. If you move on to page 4, you see who it was addressed to or to delivered to. It was signed by the federal secretary. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 22nd of April. I think I was there when the document came in. We read it, and, as was customary for the operatives in the Ministry of the Interior before the war, we were trained to act in keeping with the existing Laws on All People's Defence and the Ministry of the Interior, what to do in a war or when there is a danger of a war. But none of us were trained for an ethnic war or a civil war. There were very few inspectors there from ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, this couldn't be recorded. Please repeat the latter part of your answer when you said that members of the Ministry of the Interior were not prepared or trained. What for? Slowly, please. Slowly. It is impossible to follow.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Ministry of the Interior, in the pre-war period, were not prepared or trained for a civil war, for the eventuality of an ethnic war. Most of the operatives working with the crime police, in particular, were not properly trained for a situation in which war crimes were occurring. That is why we would have found this material helpful. When familiarising ourselves with the subject matter as well as with the institution that was now being set up, this was something that we could use to broaden our familiarity with this area. Another thing I would like to point out is about the security service centres in the pre-war period. They covered crimes against life and limb, such as murder, aggravating murder, and they -- their purpose was to shed light on crimes such as those in their own areas and our task now was to set up a total of three centres to provide some sort of training back at the HQ and train people for that type of work. In municipal bodies, the operatives mostly dealt with property-related crime. Murder, aggravating murder, and crime against life and limb were not the types of crimes that they pursued in municipal areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, the first sentence here reads: "The federal secretariat of the interior informs that at the session of the federal council held on 18th of March, 1992, the Assembly of the SFRY adopted a decision on the formation, scope, and composition of the state commission for the collection of data for verification of war crimes, crimes of genocide, and other crimes against humanity and international law committed against Serbs and other ethnicities during the armed conflict in Croatia and other parts of the country." Were you familiar with this decision of the SFRY Assembly, specifically its federal council?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiar, but not before I'd received this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did this letter impose any obligation on the ministry of the Republika Srpska; and, if so, what kind of obligation with regard to this war crimes commission? Please wait before starting your answer.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The obligation was to submit information to the Federal War Crimes Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you act pursuant to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I interpose an objection at this point. I think this is really calling for a legal conclusion on the part of this witness, whether or not the newly created Republika Srpska had any obligation to the federal Yugoslavia. Because we have had no evidence in this case that the RS was a part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept this objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let us take a look at the last page, page 4, so we may see to who this letter was distributed.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was distributed to the MUP of Serbia, of Montenegro, of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the Republic of Serbian Krajina; then to the State Commission; then to the Federal Prosecutor's Office; to the Federal Secretariat of Justice; and the Federal Secretariat of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me repeat the question. I believe that Mr. Hannis is satisfied now. Did you act pursuant to this instruction issued by the Federal Secretariat of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interject. I'm not satisfied now. The fact that Mr. Gracanin may have felt he had some control or authority over the Republika Srpska by sending this to them does not necessarily mean it existed. It may show the existence of a joint criminal enterprise but not necessarily a formal legal relationship between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska. And this witness can't testify to that. He can testify about whether or not they responded, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I suppose, though, Mr. Hannis, that it is a matter of inference. So isn't this a matter on which submissions will be made at the end of the exercise? No doubt, as I said, Mr. Zecevic will correct me if I'm wrong, but the distribution list to which the witness has been referred arising from that, there are certain inferences that he is inviting the Chamber to draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's fine, Your Honour. But my original objection was asking the witness to make an inference which I think he is not in a position to do. He is not a legal expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think I see the point, Mr. Hannis. So, Mr. Zecevic, you would rephrase the question in such a way as to avoid inviting the witness to -- to draw inferences which are properly the provenance of the Chamber. I suppose that is what Mr. Hannis' objection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My most recent objection was really just to the comment by Mr. Zecevic that I was satisfied. I really don't have an objection to his last question. It was simply put to the witness whether or not he responded to it or his agency responded to that. And that's a fair question. But I didn't feel comfortable sitting there having the Court think that I was satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So now he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I appreciate, Mr. Hannis. However, my first question before your first objection was: Did you act in accordance with this instruction, like the last question. That is my misunderstanding of your objection. I'm sorry, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Macar, the question was: Did you act pursuant to this instruction?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I understood your question in the first place. Up until October 1992, our priority was to establish a crime police administration at headquarters and establishing crime prevention services in the centres and reinforcing these compatibilities in the stations. Only later in 1993, 1994, and 1995 did the information flow toward the secretariat increase. I even attended a meeting where we exchanged experiences and received some technical assistance with regard to taking action with regard to war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When was that meeting held?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, sir, since this is a decision by the Federal Assembly of the SFRY, dated the 18th of March, 1992, tell me whether, on that day, the 18th of March, 1992, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was part of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there is an objection, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D635, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document 1D73, tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document is already in evidence, and you're familiar with it. We needn't, therefore, comment it in detail. What is the meaning of item 2 of this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP, or the minister, gives approval for conferring some duties and tasks on some persons and bodies which are listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have heard that from the very beginning, that is, the 19th of April, you were with the MUP. Tell us whether this order of the minister was implemented in practice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It often was not, probably due to the fragmentation of the territory and the influence of the Crisis Staffs in the municipalities. Many executives, such as chiefs of stations and heads of crime prevention services, did not receive approval from the minister for their appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following document is 1D150. That's tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document is one of the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was signed by Minister Alija Delimustafic. It's dated 29 April. And it relates, the decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina of 27 April. And we see it contains four items. Are you familiar with this order?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm, indeed, familiar with this document. I don't precisely remember. It was from late April or early May. But this order shows a continuity of activities that go back to the 15th of March, when the headquarters of the 2nd Army District were besieged. We had intelligence that there was observation of military facilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that there had been incidents, and this was the culmination of these activities which happened in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is late April. Were JNA members, at this time, still in their barracks and facilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the city of Sarajevo, the JNA was in its barracks and was considered a regular army. That is why such a bluntly phrased order, a war time order I may call it, was a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll show you document 1D324, MFI. That's tab 17. It's a document dated 7 May 1992 signed by the then-chief of the Bijeljina CSB, Predrag Jesuric. Tell me what -- how did you communicate with Bijeljina at that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no communication lines that could be used by the police. And sometime in April, I believe that instructions were issued that faxes should be installed to enable communication. I even think that instructions were issued that fax machines should be borrowed or supplied from the storage of the MUP, to be used for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a report which says that, due to a break in the telephone, telegraph and fax communications, during the period from the last report you didn't receive reports although they were compiled by the chief of the Bijeljina CSB. Does this report describe the situation in the territory covered by the Bijeljina CSB; and are you familiar with the document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document, just as with many others that came in from the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, how many dispatches did the crime enforcement administration send out in this initial period from about April till the end of summer 1992? Actually, how many were received at headquarters?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crime enforcement administration at the headquarters of the MUP, up until October when it moved to Bijeljina, I believe received 31 documents. Due to difficulties in communicating, also for very simple reasons, such as shortage of paper, but, more importantly because of the disorganisation in the centres that were only being established, communication was very difficult, and only very urgent dispatches were sent to the minister. But they were very few. If we take into consideration the situation on the ground. Only when technical compatibilities were enhanced and the information system became normal again, the number of documents that circulated rose again. And that can be checked by taking a look at the records that we kept from April through October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you or other administrations, depending on the subject matter, were -- were you acquainted with the contents of the dispatches received by the ministry?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the whereabouts of the individual executive. He may have been in the field at the moment. But, otherwise, we were almost in the same office at Vrace. So we had the opportunity to get acquainted with everything. But, anyway, the minister did inform us at meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When did the crime enforcement administration move to Bijeljina; and what was the reason?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, there were no resources at Pale, no materiel or technical equipment for the ministry headquarters. The same problem existed for the other ministries. There were permanent suggestions to the minister, and he agreed that it was impossible to establish the ministry headquarters there. Then a decision was taken to move the ministry to Bijeljina, in October. Let me add the following: For a considerable time in April, May, June, and part of July, some administrations were at Vrace, and they were exposed to constant shelling, sniper fire, and so on. And that's another reason why we were unable to set up normal communication and a normal functioning of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Bijeljina CSB, when was its establishment completed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On paper, the centre had been in exist earlier, but, in reality, only when the ministry arrived in Bijeljina, it took off the ground. The centre and its organisational unit started being set up from October 1992 which process ended in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, then I move that this -- the MFI mark should be removed from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the MFI qualification is taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more document before the break. That's about how much time we have. Could the witness be shown 5 -- oh, P1013, which is tab 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a dispatch of the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka, but I'm showing it to you because this dispatch reproduces in the entirety the enactment of the Serbian -- MUP of the Serbian Republic of BH, number 01-57/92. So we have the entire text of this enactment and this dispatch is sent by chief of the CSB, Stojan Zupljanin, to all public security stations. In paragraph 1, this text mentions unprincipled behaviour of the reserve policemen. Can you please explain to us, what is unprincipled behaviour of the reserve force, the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- let me first tell you that I'm familiar with this order, enactment, that was sent to all stations. I think that this was a typo. And instead of "unprincipled," there should have been "unprofessional behaviour" of the reserve force members. Whoever typed it made a mistake. I don't know whether the mistake was made at the centre or elsewhere, but the word that should have been here is "unprofessional behaviour," because we never used in our police work this phrase "unprincipled behaviour." And I remember it from the time when the order was drawn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given the time, and given the topics that I'm dealing with, I think it would be a good time for our break, as I'm about to move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we would return in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is coming in, I indicate Ms. Korner would like to address the issue of the question you had, Judge Harhoff. And I suggested that maybe we do it at the end of the day since the witness may be getting tired anyway. If we could save five minutes at the end of the day, she will come in and answer your question better than I have so far. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, yesterday, and also this morning during the first session, we touched upon some problems that you encountered in setting up the administration for crime prevention in the MUP headquarters. You mentioned problems with communication, personnel, and so on. Tell me, did you have any problems with -- with the equipment; and, if so, what kind of problems those were?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are referring to materiel and technical equipment, and I would like to mention that in the former Ministry of the Interior, the equipment procurement was a centralised process. There were forms, records, and so on. We started working from scratch. We had nothing. So starting from plain typewriters to paper, everything needed to be obtained, and we had to find a way to do it. We also needed fuel. We did not have sufficient number of vehicles, and so on. So we had to make do with friendly contacts that we had with what was left in warehouses and so on. I know that one of the colleagues brought the first typewriter, and we were overjoyed that we had something to type on. We did have some leftover typewriters but no tapes for them. And in Vrace and Pale, there were no shops selling such office supplies. Similar problems were encountered in the centres that were in the process of being established, let alone the communication system which was non-existent. We didn't have the basics. We didn't have premises. We didn't have typewriters. We didn't have the paperwork for record-keeping, and so on. And the identical situation was in the police stations. As for the equipment needed for the work of crime police, it was also non-existent. Before the war, we received our supplies on a monthly basis, and the requests were sent from centres to the ministry. And in this new situation, we lacked everything. We had no cameras. We had no film for cameras. We had no supplies needed to perform on-site investigations and work on the ground. Even before, in the centres, we had film development laboratories, because police stations would send their camera films to be developed to the centres in their film laboratories, and this no longer could be done. We needed a lot of time to set it all up. Republika Srpska was also in the process of being created. They needed a budget. There was no system of payments at the level of the country, and the minister of the interior could not provide supplies for their units. If we add to this situation the fact that the whole territory was torn into fragments and the difficult logistical situation, then you can imagine under what conditions we had to function. I apologise. Let me just mention this: That for two months, I personally, from my own funds, funded fuel for two vehicles of the Ministry of the Interior, and I don't want to mention anything smaller than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned that the territory was torn into fragments, let me show you a document, tab 35, 1D580.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please assist us with this map. Can we have the original of this map without -- without the markings, the markings of the previous witness. And we also need the entire map of Bosnia and Herzegovina. 65 ter of the Prosecution, 1013. I apologise. 65 ter 10133. My mistake; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, can you see this? It's rather small.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is it better now? With the assistance of the usher, could you please mark the headquarters of the Trebinje CSB?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphone be switched on, please. The interpreters cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please move microphones so that the interpreters can hear you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find my way on this map. Bilice, Gacko. This is not the exact territory but roughly so. This border area towards Montenegro on the one side, and Visegrad on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the area that you just circled, is that the territory in the jurisdiction of the Trebinje CSB?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the following municipalities: Trebinje, Gacko, Nevesinje, Bilice, Ljubinje, Foca, Grude, Visegrad and Cajnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communication with Foca, Grude, and Cajnice was disrupted and could only be accessed via Montenegro and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put number 1 within this circle. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell us, please, we can see where Sarajevo is, and Pale. Perhaps you could mark where Pale is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just say this: Not just Pale, but for a long time, the ministry's centre was located in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Put number 2 where the ministry's centre was located. Just take it slowly, please. Would you explain to us or draw for us the route that could be taken to the territory under the jurisdiction of the Trebinje CSB, the territory that you marked with number 1.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo, Sokolac, Han Pijesak, Maslenica, Zvornik was the only route. And then one would cross into Zmajevo, the territory of Serbia, continue on to Bajina Basta, Uzice, Novo Varos. And then one would cross into Montenegro, via Prijepolje, and then continue on via Niksic, to arrive in Trebinje. That was a road that would require 10 to 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, please, in that period of time, that is to say, April, May, June, was it possible physically to communicate with the Banja Luka and Doboj centres?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Until the corridor was -- was made accessible, it wasn't possible to reach Banja Luka or Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could you please put numbers 3 and 4, where Banja Luka and Doboj centres are.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And also underline Bijeljina, and put number 5 there to mark the fifth CSB. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise to Their Honours. If I may say that in Visegrad and Cajnice, in order to reach these areas one had to travel via Serbia. There were no direct roads to those areas, and one had to travel via Serbia to reach them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please mark the territory of Visegrad, Rudo, and Cajnice, and put an A there.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in very small letters. It's somewhere here. But I can't really see because the letters are very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there's objections, I tender to admit this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I fail to see the marking of the E. Where is it on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask for a marking by E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The last marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now it's all gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do we have it saved? Can we show it again for the benefit of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the marked map is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D636, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, did the crime squad exist throughout that period, between April and the end of summer 1992, in public security stations in the territory covered by the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most public security stations did have crime squads throughout the period. The manning levels were not sufficient though. There were some stations that had no crime squads. I do remember certain periods of time when the inspectors toured those, and they would say that they were getting some manpower from the reserve units. For the most part, the crime squads did not have appropriate manning levels. Even when they did, it wasn't consistent with the population numbers or, indeed, the extent of the problems arising throughout those areas. We also took a long time taking in the situation in its entirety that prevailed in these public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation regarding the operating legal system throughout 1992 in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were all these problems that we were encountering in our work in the MUP: Lack of equipment, low manning levels, financial problems. The legislators and the executive bodies were encountering most of the same problems. Up until the summer of 1992 or thereabouts, the prosecutors and courts were not operating throughout the RS territory. I think it wasn't before June and July the prosecutors and judges were officially and formally appointed. Now they probably took some time to set up their own operations. It required some time. But they started operating, to some extent, at least, from August that year on. The following fact corroborates just that. The Sarajevo centre had certain problems. There was a station that was part of the centre. We would have the right to keep persons in custody for up to three days and then process cases involving murders, murders of two persons or more, but there was no one to file our criminal reports with. I remember that sometime, like, June or July that year, I toured the Sarajevo area, Sokolac, Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, just to see whether there was a properly operating prosecutor's office, where, regardless of their respective jurisdictions, I could submit a criminal report, until such time as proper prosecutors in courts were set up in Sarajevo. We had some problems with the citizens and the people we arrested, too. We could only keep them for up to three days. So, obviously, when they saw those people at large again after three days in such neighbourhoods and towns, people would protest and obviously they would voice their displeasure and direct their anger at the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you provided a brief comment in relation to one of the documents that I showed you in the earlier course of your evidence. Was there any local influence being exerted on any local officers of the Ministry of the Interior throughout the territory? How did that materialise?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most of those, the -- there was appreciable influence of the local authorities and the Crisis Staffs. This concerned the fundamental logistics issues as well as their salaries, which they received from the municipal bodies. The municipal Crisis Staffs affected the appointments that were made, and the persons who were appointed to all of the leading positions in the police stations and crime squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How long did that problem persist for, from the perspective of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having toward some of the territory --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please focus on my question. How long for? That was my question. Could you give us a time-frame.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of the problem was resolved -- well, actually, not resolved but the conditions were created to resolve it. We abolished the autonomous regions and also the Crisis Staffs, although there were still some ramifications that persisted for some time afterwards. We tried to take all of these things in our stride and deal with it as we went along in order to restore the influence of the ministry itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, for the umpteenth time, please, speak slowly. It is quite physically impossible to follow what you are saying because of the speed and I can only imagine how hard the interpreters must find it. It is recorded here that you said, "We abolished the autonomous regions and the Crisis Staffs." Who and when abolished the autonomous regions in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decisions were political, and they were decisions taken by the government of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether constitutional amendments were made in that regard, that is, to abolish the autonomous regions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that. That was a prerequisite to have those abolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, properly speaking, when that occurred? What year, what period of time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when the decision was taken to abolish the Crisis Staffs? What time-period, what year?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1992. I think sometime in September, if memory serves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you've enumerated all these problems for us, the problems that you were encountering in your work. Did people at the Ministry of the Interior discuss these problems?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At collegium meetings and briefings at the HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you attend any of these collegium meetings and briefings?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you adopt any conclusions regarding these problems?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means we would provide opinions and proposals, table those to the minister. There would be discussions, and then conclusions were adopted, as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Any conclusions in relation to the situation regarding the influence of the local bodies of government on the local units of the Ministry of the Interior, specifically the public security stations; and, if so, what conclusions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was debated at the collegium meetings and the reporting sessions of the Administration of the crime investigation police. Especially after touring the public security stations further afield, we informed the minister that the Crisis Staffs were overbearingly influential. When one arrived in those areas, most of the leaders were members of the Crisis Staffs. They would tell us directly that they had been receiving orders from the Crisis Staffs to carry out certain tasks and missions. It was based on decisions taken by the Crisis Staffs that police officers were sent to the front line too.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Can the witness please repeat the figures that he has just mentioned. Thank you. We didn't catch those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... repeat the figures that you just mentioned. Can you please repeat the figures, because the interpreters didn't catch it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 70 and 80 percent of police officers, particularly throughout the Sarajevo area, were deployed to the front line within the armed forces of the RS. And their deployment there was at the request of the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In a purely functional sense, how did that situation affect the Ministry of the Interior of the RS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of our conclusions was this: The heads of the public security stations should, as a matter of priority, inform the Crisis Staffs of their work. And for the most part, they weren't informing the Security Services Centre or the Ministry of the Interior in situations where that was required. There are two aspects to this. One was a technical aspect. It was physically impossible to communicate with the centre, or the minister, the HQ. That is part of the reason why they had to communicate with the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In a functional sense, how did this affect the work of the ministry? So what I want to know is this: Could the ministry establish a functional hierarchy in keeping with the law?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, most of the people in the leading positions, the chiefs and heads of public security stations, were never appointed by the minister but by the local Crisis Staffs, which is why they believed that they should prioritise their reporting to the Crisis Staffs, the bodies that previously appointed them to their positions. I think that is probably one of the most important reasons why the ministry, or, rather, the security centres were unable to have a consistent subordination system, in terms of the way they functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, 1D84 is our next document. This is tab 24. Signed by Dobro Planojevic; date, the 5th of June, 1992. Are you familiar with this, sir? What is this about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with it. Mr. Planojevic and I had a chance, throughout this period of time, to discuss security-related information. This document was produced on that basis. The document is a reminder and a guide-line to the centres and stations, public security stations, in terms of what approach they should take to certain cases. A portion of this document discusses steps that were taken to combat crime and certain deviations committed by members of the police that had been observed. Another portion of the document talks about the need to act and the ways in which to act when documenting war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "documenting war crimes," did the Ministry of the Interior distinguish between cases involving different ethnic affiliations of the perpetrators and the victims?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior, starting from the minister to the crime enforcement administration, to other administrations, such as the police administration, when we discussed war crimes, we included crimes committed against any inhabitants of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, regardless of their ethnic affiliation. Any documents about that were sent to public security centres, and these forwarded them to the public security stations in their territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To illustrate what you're saying, let us take a look at 113D1, which is under tab 28. This is a letter of Jovo Cokorilo, chief of CSB, which he sent to public security stations. The CSB in question is that of Trebinje and the date is 24 June 1992. It says: "We received the following document from the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then the contents of that document received from the ministry is -- are stated. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document forwarded to the public security stations, and this is about an enactment sent out by Mr. Planojevic. I know Jovo Cokorilo. He was a very conscientious chief, and I note that the document signed by Mr. Planojevic is dated 5 June 1992; whereas, Mr. Cokorilo's document is dated 24 June. We have just discussed the difficulties in communication and how difficult it was to forward documents in a timely fashion, and this is another illustration of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document, unless this is an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understood -- I'm sorry, I thought it was already in. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D637, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about this, we were able to see from a number of documents shown in this trial that sometimes war crimes committed against Serbs are singled out. Can you tell us if you know anything about this; and, if you do, what was the reason?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know about this. The reason why information was requested from public security centres and public security stations was because a report had to be drawn up, pursuant to the request of a government body. I think it was the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and possibly for the Presidency, too. But I'm sure about the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. In 1992, there was much propaganda. The Serbs were represented in various ways, very bad ways, which you probably know. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs wanted to present the situation on the ground as realistically as possible. That's why we compiled information for this report to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These war crimes against Serbs, were they committed in the territory controlled by the RS MUP or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most part of the information that we submitted to the ministry was about crimes committed in areas controlled by Muslim or Croatian forces. Since there were many such -- since there was -- there were many people that had come or that were coming from those areas, we also received information about these crimes and their perpetrators. Where we did not have pertinent information, we filed criminal complaints against unknown perpetrators, or, if we were unable to obtain good evidence, we would make Official Notes to be dealt with at a time when we get more evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have information concerning the war crimes committed against Serbs in territories controlled by Muslim or Croatian forces that they were processed by the judicial bodies in those territories?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP collected much evidence and many criminal complaints were submitted, but I don't know of any one such case being processed. Even now, only a few cases are being dealt with by the judicial bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although hundreds of files have been submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have been able to see a number of criminal complaints for war crimes. It was stated here in this court that crimes committed by Muslims or Croats against Serbs were treated as war crimes; whereas, in similar situations, when Serbs committed such crimes against members of other ethnicities, the MUP treated such crimes as aggravated murder or some other type of murder but not as a war crime. Can you comment on the reasons, if you know them? Just wait for my question to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I refuse, with determination, any claim that the MUP acted in the fashion that you described, with premeditation. The public security stations and public security centres submitted criminal complaints for war crimes when they had information that a war crime had been committed and whenever they were able to collect evidence to support their complaint. When there were murders of individuals or more persons, when the motive of the murder was unknown, or when the motivation was personal gain, and such crimes were committed against Serbs, too, there were even perpetrators who did these things against anybody, regardless of ethnicity. And I repeat, these were murders or aggravated robbery with lethal outcome --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat your last sentence, sir.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The characterisation of these crimes was not such, or motivated by the desire to qualify crimes against one ethnicity as being one type of crime rather than another. The qualification depended on the information, or the evidence, that the public security station or the public security centre had been able to gather. Let me add that the qualification of the security services was not binding upon the prosecutor. Because the latter, having received a criminal complaint, or upon completion of an investigation, could re-qualify that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "qualify," you mean label a crime in an indictment.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in an indictment. When a criminal complaint was submitted to the prosecutor's office, which was due process, when a crime was committed, even with premeditation, that labelling was not binding on the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand as much, sir. But you say -- you said "qualification." Do you mean the determination of the type of crime which was used by the prosecutor in the indictment? And I say "indictment" because that's the basis for criminal proceedings before a court. That's why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I understand your question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we would take the break now and return in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I don't know whether this was communicated to you, but Ms. Korner has indicated that 20 minutes she would need, so you would pace yourself accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The last session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In the last session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, at page 28 of the LiveNote, one of your answers during the last session, we talked about these problems being discussed at collegium meetings and briefings that were held, the problems that you were encountering in your work, that you identified in your work, and then the problems were presented at briefings and collegium meetings of the ministry, at the ministry's HQ. Based on your knowledge, did the local Crisis Staffs pay their salaries to the members of local public security stations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. In most cases, due to the fact that the budget and payment systems were not functioning, local municipal organs, that is to say, Crisis Staffs, paid salaries and provided materiel and technical equipment to the SJBs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 614, tab 23, please. 614D1, please, tab 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, this is a conclusion reached by the Prijedor Crisis Staff, signed by Dr. Milomir Stakic. The date is 5th of June, 1992. And this document is entitled: "Conclusion on the method of calculation and payment of salaries, organisations," and so on, for the month of May. Do you know that such and similar documents were issued by Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about this. I know that by way of their decisions and pursuant to requests for supplies, et cetera, from the SJBs, the Crisis Staffs would pay their salaries and other types of materiel and technical equipment. Under item 1 here, we see that they mention paying out salaries. And here we see that they had a provision that the families of those who had gone missing or were in prison would receive salaries for the missing persons. It says here in this conclusion that the public security stations needed to issue receipts for the monies received.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do have an objection. The witness said he is familiar with these kind of documents, but there is no indication that he was ever at the Prijedor Crisis Staff or knows Dr. Stakic or whether this was issued, or the basis of his claimed information about Crisis Staffs. We haven't heard any foundation about his source of information about knowing what Crisis Staffs did and when they did it and how they did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Zecevic, may I add a question about the relevance of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours it precisely show what the witness's testimony is about, that the Crisis Staffs -- it confirms that the Crisis Staffs were paying the salaries of the ministries -- of the SJBs, local SJBs, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is that a contested issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it is, based on the objection from Mr. Hannis. Because it is my understanding that Mr. Hannis does not agree with --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My objection about this particulars document is more a general objection, just evidentiary wise. This witness wasn't in Prijedor, wasn't a member of the Crisis Staff, doesn't know anything about it. So this is not the appropriate witness to put this document in through. As far as whether some Crisis Staffs paid some policemen at sometime during 1992, I don't think that is an issue. We have alleged a joint criminal enterprise between the police and the political structures in the army. So in that regard, it doesn't matter to us so much, but it is just a specific evidentiary point about this document with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, on what basis do you know this? How do you know about the influence that the local Crisis Staffs had on the local SJBs? You said that you discussed it in collegium meetings and in briefings within the ministry. But, please, tell me, how do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first concrete information I received was in the meetings that I attended in the territory of the Sarajevo Security Centre, as well as from the inspectors of the administration who went to inspect certain SJBs. As for Prijedor, throughout 1992 and partially in 1993, they were paid by the municipality. And I learned about this in early 1993, when we had our first meeting with the -- with the management, with the senior leadership of the Prijedor station. In most of the municipalities, it was the Crisis Staff who paid salaries to the members of the SJB, to the staff workers of the SJB, in their territory, and also provided other types of support, such as fuel and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I hope that I have been able to clarify now the origin of the knowledge that the witness has about these specific matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, once again, I tendered this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't object. I will address it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D638, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, at the headquarters of the ministry, did you have any information about the relationship between the local Crisis Staff with their respective local SJBs; and, if so, where did that information come from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the ministry headquarters and in the administration where I worked, we did have information about the influence that the Crisis Staffs had over the SJBs and the senior staff members in the stations. This information mostly came from the reports that we received and also came from the information gathered while either inspectors or staff members from other organs came to inspect SJBs. In late 1992, I personally had occasion to see in Prijedor what influence the Crisis Staff there had over the Prijedor SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We will come to that later. Tell me, did you know that local Crisis Staffs, given the relationship between Crisis Staffs and SJBs, issued certain instructions and orders that the SJBs were to carry out?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we have some specification as to the time-frame for this. Because there's been much made of the fact that there were no communications. Phone lines weren't working, and yet he has all this information about the Crisis Staffs. So are we talking about 1993, late 1992, April, May, June? Some specification, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you have heard the Prosecutor. Tell us, please, about the time-frame, when you received this information.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information concerning the influence that the Crisis Staffs had and also orders that they issued to SJBs came to me already in June or July, when the first inspections by inspectors started in the administration of crime police, and also inspections of CSBs. This was in the Sarajevo region first, and then, starting in October onwards, in the Doboj area, and then in March, as I have said, in the Krajina region, especially in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In March of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will now show you a document, 619D1 [Realtime transcript read in error "691D1"], which is tab 57. Before we look at the document, Mr. Macar, let me ask you this: Do you know whether, in 1992, local Crisis Staffs changed their names, changed their composition, in terms of membership; and do you know what they were called?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, sometime until September/October 1992, they were known as Crisis Staff. And later on, they were known, I think, as War Presidencies, or War Commissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, just for the record, you asked to see document 691.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 619D1. It's tab 57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just get it the right for the record. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this document has a heading: "A summary of conclusions adopted by Prijedor municipality Executive Committee relating to the public security service and regional command from 29 April to 17 August 1992." It is signed by the Crisis Staff/War Presidency. And here we see the conclusions that the Crisis Staff or the Executive Committee of Prijedor submitted to the public security station. Do you know, and, if so, how do you know, that such conclusions were sent by the Executive Committee of Prijedor to the public security station to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was am incident which took place in Prijedor sometime in November, and that caused me to look into the situation and the conduct of senior staff members. When we had a meeting in March, I inquired into how the public security station in Prijedor functioned because there had already been some indicia back in November that the command was in the hands of the Crisis Staff, or War Presidency. In March, I was surprised to hear that regular, routine police duties and tasks that are normally performed by SJBs or CSBs were taken over by the Crisis Staff and regular police -- we're talking about regular police tasks that SJBs is supposed to carry out in co-ordination with the centre. That was the first time I saw how a municipal organ or body interfered in the work of the SJB. It was normal for a SJB to inform about the situation in the territory of the municipality, but it wasn't normal for a Crisis Staff to criticise its work, and it wasn't normal for a SJB to receive orders and instructions from any municipal organ. For me, it was simply incomprehensible at the time. However, it did confirm the information that we started receiving back in July and October about the situation on the ground in Republika Srpska. However, I had no idea that had -- they interfered to this extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify the time. What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you say that these problems were discussed at collegium meetings and briefings at the ministry's HQ. You said this at page 28. The minister was kept informed about these things. Do you know, and, if so, how do you know, do you have anything indicating that, at the time, the minister took any steps to deal with these problems that were raised at collegium meetings and briefings? Did he contact any state bodies or other bodies about this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that the minister informed the government, based on information received from all the various administrations, particularly from the police, the crime police, and probably the state security bodies, too. I know that this was one of the topics discussed at the government meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any steps were taken about this or, indeed, any measures? Did the government do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think soon after the information was received and spread, the autonomous regions and Crisis Staffs were abolished. I'm not sure which was abolished first, the one or the other. But both things took no longer than a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you spoke about the following problem: There was no functional legal system in place, or judicial system in place. What about the military courts? The military judicial? I'm talking about the period between April and the end of summer of 1992. Were those operating? First of all, did that exist at all throughout the period specified?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, up until August, the same problems persisted as in relation to the civilian judiciary and courts. The same situation applied to the military plain. I think they only started operating sometime in August, the military prosecutors and judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What implications, if any, did that fact have vis-a-vis the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The non-existence of judicial bodies, specifically the prosecutors, obviously, was a source of difficulties in the work of the RS police, particularly the crime police. There were a number of serious crimes where it was necessary to confirm with the prosecutors, inform them of any crimes that were -- serious crimes that were committed and get advice on what to do. There were no prosecutors in some areas covered by existing public security stations. There was also the problem of the respective jurisdictions, civilian and military, because there were no military prosecutors. Throughout this period, the public security stations had no choice but to simply register certain events but were still unable to forward cases to a prosecutor. Cases were filed in the hope that such a time would arrive, when military prosecutors would start operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say registered certain events in the hope that once the military judicial bodies got off the ground, appropriate criminal reports could be submitted and filed. What about the MUP of the Republika Srpska of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did the MUP have a list of standardised formats, documents, that were required for the work of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Standardised formats and documents existed that were supposed to be used by all of the SJBs and CSBs, ranging from criminal form, the format used by crime police and the forensic people, and a number of other modules and forms that were used in the work of the crime police. In particular, forms to be filled in when people's flats were searched, person's vehicles were searched to seize, when persons were searched, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were all these various forms and documents prescribed, in terms of an existing standard or norm, and were these really available in SJBs under the MUP of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would normally be certain decisions, provisions and instructions prescribing the format. As for the actual supplies of equipment, stationary, including log-books and forms, this worked in a centralised basis. From the Ministry of the Interior of the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, all these were printed in one place, and certain stations had old stocks, so to speak. But there wasn't too much of that to go around because this had to be printed on a monthly basis. So they were using up their old stocks. Most of the stations were encountering difficulties regarding the availability of these log-books for criminal reports and other types of forms. So we wanted to have more of all of those for the work of the crime police, and we wanted these documents to be reprinted, new copies to be printed. I think it wasn't before the end of 1992 that we started printing new copies and distributing these forms and documents to the SJBs throughout the territory. There's one thing that I would like to add: Those CSBs that were being set up had nothing in stock, not a single sheet of paper. They had none of those documents because they were just being in the process of being established. That is why the SJBs and the centres had no choice but to keep provisional records and to use ordinary notebooks to keep these records.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about the so-called KU log-book? Would that be one of those documents?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was the first time those were printed to meet the needs of the RS BiH MUP, specifically?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think sometime late in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How did it work up until that time? Based on what you know, how were records kept in the SJBs and CSBs that had no forms to use?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the versatility of those working there. Some were using ordinary notebooks. Some were simply biding their time, waiting to receive the right formats and documents so they could start keeping their records. It really depended on their resourcefulness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This was a small digression. And now I'm going back to the issue of military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 566D1, tab 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the date here is the 24 of August 1992. Notification on the commencement of the work of the military court and military prosecutor's office. To: The Ministry of the Interior, signed by Assistant Commander Ljuban Kosovac. If you turn the page, you will find the document itself. It's got a handwritten portion there. First of all, have you seen this document, sir; and, second of all, can you comment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document. All the SJBs and CSBs, particularly the crime squads there, were to be informed of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The handwritten addition there, in the upper right corner, Pero, addressed to, and so on and so forth, and then someone's signature there. Can you sled some light on that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pero was head of the analytics department. On behalf of the MUP, he is sending this to the Sarajevo CSB, and they're supposed to then inform the SJBs.
